questions.stem: Which description matches the model of the atom used in chemistry today?
options: A dense core of electrons, surrounded by a cloud of protons and neutrons
A tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in energy levels around it
A sphere of positive charge with electrons spread evenly through all of it
A nucleus of protons and electrons, with neutrons moving in shells around it
questions.explanation: Almost all the mass is in a very small nucleus of protons and neutrons, and the electrons occupy energy levels around it. A sphere of positive charge with embedded electrons is Thomson's earlier plum pudding model, which the gold foil experiment overturned.

questions.stem: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
options: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of each of its atoms
The number of electrons in the outer shell of each atom
The number of protons in the nucleus of each of its atoms
The total number of protons and neutrons in each nucleus
questions.explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons, which defines the element. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, which differs between isotopes of the same element.

questions.stem: When alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil, most passed straight through but a very few bounced back. What did this show about the atom?
options: It contains neutral particles with about the same mass as the proton
Its positive charge and most of its mass are in a tiny central nucleus
Its electrons occupy fixed energy levels at set distances from the centre
Its positive charge is spread evenly through the whole volume of the atom
questions.explanation: Most particles passing through shows the atom is mostly empty space; the rare large deflections need a small, dense, positive centre. Energy levels came from Bohr's later work on spectra, not from this experiment.

questions.stem: Bohr's model placed electrons in fixed energy levels. Which observation did this model explain that earlier models could not?
options: Hydrogen emits light only at a few particular wavelengths
Atoms of one element can have different mass numbers
Most of the mass of an atom is found in its nucleus
Alpha particles pass straight through thin metal foil
questions.explanation: If electrons can only have certain energies, they can only emit light whose energy matches the gap between two levels, giving a line spectrum. Different mass numbers (isotopes) are explained by neutrons, which were discovered later.

questions.stem: The neutron was discovered decades after the electron and the proton. Which property of the neutron made it harder to detect?
options: It orbits far outside the nucleus, well beyond the outermost electrons
It has no charge, so it is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields
Its mass is so much smaller than a proton's that it could not be measured
It exists only in the nuclei of the heaviest elements, such as uranium
questions.explanation: Charged particles betray themselves by bending in electric and magnetic fields; a neutral particle does not. The neutron's mass is in fact very close to the proton's, and every nucleus except hydrogen-1 contains neutrons.

questions.stem: What produces the bright lines in the emission spectrum of an element?
options: Protons in the nucleus changing into neutrons and releasing energy
Atoms losing all of their electrons as they are heated in the flame
Electrons dropping from higher to lower energy levels and releasing light
Electrons absorbing light and jumping from lower to higher energy levels
questions.explanation: Heating excites electrons to higher levels; when they fall back, each drop releases light of one particular energy and so one wavelength. Electrons absorbing light and moving up produces dark lines in an absorption spectrum.

questions.stem: Why is the emission spectrum of an element a set of separate lines instead of a continuous band of colour?
options: Each electron in the atom gives one line, so there is a line per electron
The prism in the spectroscope blocks the wavelengths between the lines
Electrons can have only certain energies, so only certain energy gaps exist
The flame reaches only certain temperatures, so only certain colours form
questions.explanation: Because the energy levels are distinct, only particular differences in energy are possible, and each corresponds to one wavelength. The number of lines is not the number of electrons: one electron can make many different transitions.

questions.stem: Sodium vapour absorbs light at exactly the wavelengths of the bright lines in sodium's emission spectrum. Why are the wavelengths the same?
options: Sodium absorbs every wavelength except those it is able to emit
Absorbed light is re-emitted with exactly double its original energy
Absorption and emission both happen in the nucleus of the sodium atom
Both involve electrons moving between the same pairs of energy levels
questions.explanation: An electron absorbs the energy needed to move up between two levels and releases the same energy when it falls back between them, so the wavelengths match. Both processes involve electrons, not the nucleus.

questions.stem: Sunlight passed through a spectroscope shows dark lines (Fraunhofer lines) across the continuous spectrum. What causes most of these lines?
options: Wavelengths that the sun's hot core is not able to produce at all
Sunspots blocking light of particular colours from reaching Earth
Elements in the sun emitting much more strongly at those wavelengths
Elements in the sun's outer layers absorbing particular wavelengths
questions.explanation: Atoms in the cooler outer layers absorb light at the wavelengths of their own transitions, leaving dark lines. Strong emission would produce bright lines, not dark ones. Matching these lines to known elements reveals the sun's composition.

questions.stem: Helium was identified in the spectrum of the sun before it was found on Earth. What made this identification possible?
options: Helium's lines were brighter than those of every other element
Helium was the only element whose lines appeared in sunlight
Helium's lines fell exactly halfway between two hydrogen lines
A spectral line in sunlight matched no element then known on Earth
questions.explanation: Every element has its own set of wavelengths, so a line that matched no known element pointed to a new one. Many elements, including hydrogen, also show lines in sunlight, so helium was not unique in appearing there.

questions.stem: Bunsen and Kirchhoff found new lines in the spectra of mineral water and a mineral, which led them to discover two new elements. Which elements were they?
options: Caesium and rubidium
Helium and neon
Sodium and potassium
Argon and krypton
questions.explanation: Their spectroscope revealed unfamiliar blue lines (caesium) and red lines (rubidium), showing that spectra could detect elements present in tiny amounts. Sodium and potassium were already known from the early 1800s.

questions.stem: A solution gives a lilac flame in a flame test. Which metal ion is it most likely to contain?
options: Copper
Calcium
Potassium
Sodium
questions.explanation: Potassium ions give a lilac flame. Sodium gives an intense yellow-orange flame, copper a blue-green flame and calcium an orange-red flame.

questions.stem: A fireworks maker wants an intense red colour. Which compound should be added to the mixture?
options: Sodium nitrate
Copper nitrate
Potassium nitrate
Strontium nitrate
questions.explanation: Strontium's strongest emission lines are in the red part of the spectrum. Sodium compounds give yellow-orange, copper gives blue-green and potassium a pale lilac.

questions.stem: Some elements give no visible colour in a flame test, even though their electrons are excited by the heat. Why?
options: Their electrons fall back to lower levels without releasing energy
They have no electrons that can move to a higher energy level
They emit all visible wavelengths equally, so no colour is seen
Their electron transitions release light outside the visible range
questions.explanation: Energy is always released when an excited electron falls back, but for many elements the energy gaps correspond to ultraviolet or infrared light, which the eye cannot see. Every atom has electrons that can be excited.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same number of which particle but different numbers of which particle?
options: Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
Same number of neutrons, different numbers of protons
Same number of electrons, different numbers of protons
Same number of protons, different numbers of electrons
questions.explanation: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; isotopes differ only in their neutrons and so in mass number. Atoms with different numbers of electrons are ions, not isotopes.

questions.stem: How many neutrons are in an atom of ⁵⁶₂₆Fe?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 56 − 26 = 30. The 26 is the number of protons, and 82 comes from adding the two numbers instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: An atom has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. How is it written in isotope notation?
options: ¹⁷₃₇Cl
³⁷₁₇Cl
²⁰₁₇Cl
³⁷₂₀Ca
questions.explanation: The mass number (17 + 20 = 37) goes at the top left and the atomic number (17) at the bottom left; 17 protons makes it chlorine. Twenty is the number of neutrons, not the atomic number, so it is not calcium.

questions.stem: A particle has 20 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons. How is it written?
options: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁻
³⁸₂₀Ca²⁺
⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺
⁴⁰₁₈Ar
questions.explanation: Twenty protons makes it calcium; the mass number is 20 + 20 = 40; two fewer electrons than protons gives a 2+ charge. A 2− charge would need two extra electrons, and argon-40 would have 18 protons, not 20.

questions.stem: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 can be separated by the slightly different rates at which their gaseous fluorides diffuse, but not by chemical reactions. Why?
options: Only uranium-238 forms a gaseous compound with fluorine
They differ in mass but have the same arrangement of electrons
They differ in protons but have exactly the same atomic mass
They differ in electrons but have exactly the same nucleus
questions.explanation: Chemical properties depend on electron arrangement, which is the same for all isotopes of an element, so reactions cannot tell them apart. The extra three neutrons make uranium-238 heavier, which changes physical properties such as diffusion rate.

questions.stem: Which use of a radioisotope is matched correctly?
options: Carbon-14 to estimate the age of once-living material
Carbon-12 to estimate the age of once-living material
Hydrogen-1 as a radioactive tracer in medical imaging
Oxygen-16 as a radioactive tracer in plant studies
questions.explanation: Living things take in carbon-14, which decays at a known rate after death, so the amount left indicates age. Carbon-12, hydrogen-1 and oxygen-16 are stable isotopes, so they are not radioactive and cannot act as radioactive tracers.

questions.stem: Boron is 19.9% boron-10 (relative isotopic mass 10.01) and 80.1% boron-11 (11.01). What is the relative atomic mass of boron?
questions.explanation: Weighted mean = 0.199 × 10.01 + 0.801 × 11.01 = 1.99 + 8.82 = 10.81. A simple average gives 10.51, and swapping the abundances gives 10.21.

questions.stem: Gallium has two isotopes, of relative isotopic mass 68.93 and 70.92, and a relative atomic mass of 69.72. What is the percentage abundance of the lighter isotope?
questions.explanation: Let x be the fraction of the lighter isotope: 68.93x + 70.92(1 − x) = 69.72, so 1.99x = 1.20 and x = 0.603. The answer 39.7% is the heavier isotope's share; 69.72 lies closer to 68.93, so the lighter isotope must be the more abundant.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of an element shows peaks at mass 24 (79%), 25 (10%) and 26 (11%). Taking each isotope's relative mass as its mass number, what is the relative atomic mass?
questions.explanation: Weighted mean = 0.79 × 24 + 0.10 × 25 + 0.11 × 26 = 18.96 + 2.50 + 2.86 = 24.32. A plain average of 24, 25 and 26 gives 25.0, which ignores the much higher abundance of mass 24.

questions.stem: Which is the subshell electron configuration of a sulfur atom, which has 16 electrons?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁸ 3s² 3p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3d⁴
questions.explanation: The subshells fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, giving 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16 electrons. A 2p subshell holds at most 6 electrons, and 3p⁶ would total 18 electrons, which is the sulfide ion.

questions.stem: Which is the subshell electron configuration of a potassium atom (19 electrons)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4p¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
questions.explanation: The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: the 19th electron goes into 4s. This fits potassium's place in group 1, with one outer electron like sodium.

questions.stem: Which is the subshell electron configuration of an iron atom (26 electrons)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁸
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁴ 4s² 4p²
questions.explanation: After argon's 18 electrons, 4s fills with 2 and then 3d takes the remaining 6. Putting 4p electrons in before 3d is full ignores the filling order; iron is a d-block element.

questions.stem: Strontium has atomic number 38. Which is its subshell electron configuration?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶ 5s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶ 4d²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴ 5s² 5p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁸ 4s² 4p⁶ 5s² 5p²
questions.explanation: After 4p⁶ (krypton, 36 electrons), the 5s subshell is lower in energy than 4d, so the last two electrons go into 5s. This matches strontium's place in group 2 and period 5.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in a d subshell, and in the whole third shell?
options: 5 in a d subshell and 9 in the third shell
10 in a d subshell and 18 in the third shell
10 in a d subshell and 8 in the third shell
6 in a d subshell and 18 in the third shell
questions.explanation: A d subshell has five orbitals of two electrons each, so 10. The third shell has 3s (2), 3p (6) and 3d (10), totalling 18. Eight is the number in the third shell of argon, before 3d starts filling.

questions.stem: An atom has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵. Where is the element in the periodic table?
options: Period 4, group 15, in the p-block
Period 4, group 7, in the d-block
Period 4, group 17, in the p-block
Period 5, group 17, in the p-block
questions.explanation: The highest shell occupied is the fourth, so it is in period 4; seven outer electrons (4s² 4p⁵) place it in group 17; the last electron enters a p subshell. This is bromine. The full 3d subshell does not make it a d-block element.

questions.stem: In the modern periodic table, the elements are arranged in order of increasing:
options: relative atomic mass
number of neutrons
electronegativity
atomic number
questions.explanation: Elements are ordered by the number of protons. Ordering by atomic mass, as in early tables, put a few pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, in the wrong groups.

questions.stem: Why did Mendeleev's periodic table become widely accepted by chemists?
options: He ordered every element strictly by increasing atomic mass, with no exceptions
He used the electron configuration of each element to place it in a group
He arranged the elements by atomic number, which he was the first to measure
He left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements, later confirmed
questions.explanation: His predictions for missing elements, such as the one later named germanium, matched their properties when they were found. He did swap some pairs against the mass order to keep groups consistent, and electrons and atomic numbers were not known in his time.

questions.stem: How does atomic radius change across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, and why?
options: It stays the same, as every atom in period 3 has three shells
It decreases, as more protons pull electrons in the same shell closer
It increases, as each element has more electrons that take up space
It decreases, as each element adds an extra shell of electrons
questions.explanation: Across a period, electrons are added to the same outer shell while the nuclear charge rises, so the outer electrons are held closer. New shells are added going down a group, not across a period.

questions.stem: Which of these atoms has the largest radius?
options: Chlorine
Potassium
Sodium
Magnesium
questions.explanation: Radius increases down a group and decreases across a period. Potassium has four occupied shells, while sodium, magnesium and chlorine have three, and of those sodium is largest.

questions.stem: Electronegativities are Na 0.9, Mg 1.2, Al 1.5, P 2.1 and Cl 3.2. Which statement describes and explains this trend?
options: It rises across the period as the atoms become larger and hold electrons more loosely
It rises across the period as metals attract shared electrons more than non-metals
It rises across the period as the nuclear charge attracting bonding electrons increases
It rises across the period as each atom has more shells shielding the outer electrons
questions.explanation: Across a period the atoms get smaller and the nuclear charge increases, so they attract a shared pair of electrons more strongly. The number of shells stays the same across a period, and the atoms get smaller, not larger.

questions.stem: Why does electronegativity decrease down group 17 from fluorine to iodine?
options: Each atom lower in the group has fewer electrons in its outer shell
Larger atoms have more protons, which repel shared bonding electrons
Bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells
The nuclear charge decreases down the group, attracting bonding electrons less
questions.explanation: Each step down adds a shell, so the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is screened by more inner electrons. The nuclear charge actually increases down the group, and every group 17 atom has seven outer electrons.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the valencies of Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S and Cl in their compounds with hydrogen?
questions.explanation: The hydrides are NaH, MgH₂, AlH₃, SiH₄, PH₃, H₂S and HCl. Up to group 14 the valency equals the number of outer electrons; after that it is the number of electrons needed to fill the outer shell (8 minus the number of outer electrons).

questions.stem: An element has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. What is its valency, and which compound does it form with hydrogen?
options: Valency 5, forming PH₅
Valency 3, forming P₃H
Valency 2, forming PH₂
Valency 3, forming PH₃
questions.explanation: With five outer electrons, phosphorus shares three more to reach eight, so it forms three bonds, as in PH₃. Writing P₃H reverses the ratio of the atoms.

questions.stem: Which of these elements is in the d-block of the periodic table?
options: Bromine
Uranium
Iron
Calcium
questions.explanation: The d-block holds groups 3 to 12, where d subshells are filling; iron is in group 8. Calcium is in the s-block, bromine in the p-block and uranium in the f-block.

questions.stem: Group 14 runs from carbon, a non-metal, through silicon and germanium to tin and lead, which are metals. Which explanation fits this trend?
options: Lower elements have fewer protons, so their electrons are attracted less
Larger atoms lose their valence electrons more easily, so metallic character rises
Larger atoms have higher electronegativity, so metallic character rises
Lower elements have more valence electrons, so they form more metallic bonds
questions.explanation: Down a group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily, which is typical of metals. Electronegativity falls, not rises, down a group, and all group 14 atoms have four valence electrons.

questions.stem: Element Q has an electronegativity of 0.9 and its atoms are larger than magnesium atoms. Where is Q most likely to be found?
options: Group 2, in period 2 of the table
Group 16, in period 3 of the table
Group 17, in period 4 of the table
Group 1, in period 3 or a lower period
questions.explanation: Low electronegativity and a large radius point to the far left of the table and not near the top. Beryllium in group 2, period 2 is smaller than magnesium, and groups 16 and 17 have high electronegativities.
